claim: In vitro Mu transposition was used to generate a random truncation library of NRC4.
source: We used in vitro Mu transposition to generate a random truncation library and identify the minimal functional region of NLRs. We applied this method to NRC4—a helper NLR that functions with multiple sensor NLRs within a Solanaceae receptor network.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental method used to generate the truncation library.

claim: The N-terminal 29 amino acids of NRC4 are sufficient to induce hypersensitive cell death.
source: This revealed that the NRC4 N-terminal 29 amino acids are sufficient to induce hypersensitive cell death.
evidence: The abstract states this finding directly, and it is supported by experimental data shown in the results.

claim: The MADA motif is defined by the consensus sequence MADAxVSFxVxKLxxLLxxEx.
source: This region is defined by the consensus MADAxVSFxVxKLxxLLxxEx (MADA motif) that is conserved at the N-termini of NRC family proteins and ~20% of coiled-coil (CC)-type plant NLRs.
evidence: The consensus sequence is explicitly stated in the abstract and derived from computational analysis.

claim: The MADA motif is conserved at the N-termini of NRC family proteins and approximately 20% of coiled-coil (CC)-type plant NLRs.
source: This region is defined by the consensus MADAxVSFxVxKLxxLLxxEx (MADA motif) that is conserved at the N-termini of NRC family proteins and ~20% of coiled-coil (CC)-type plant NLRs.
evidence: The abstract provides this quantitative finding based on bioinformatic analysis.

claim: The MADA motif matches the N-terminal α1 helix of Arabidopsis NLR protein ZAR1.
source: The MADA motif matches the N-terminal α1 helix of Arabidopsis NLR protein ZAR1, which undergoes a conformational switch during resistosome activation.
evidence: The abstract states this structural correspondence, which is supported by sequence alignment and structural modeling in the results.

claim: The α1 helix of ZAR1 undergoes a conformational switch during resistosome activation.
source: The MADA motif matches the N-terminal α1 helix of Arabidopsis NLR protein ZAR1, which undergoes a conformational switch during resistosome activation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and references prior structural studies by Wang et al. (2019b).

claim: The MADA motif is functionally conserved across NLRs from distantly related plant species.
source: Immunoassays revealed that the MADA motif is functionally conserved across NLRs from distantly related plant species.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, which is supported by motif swap experiments in the results.

claim: NRC-dependent sensor NLRs lack MADA sequences.
source: NRC-dependent sensor NLRs lack MADA sequences indicating that this motif has degenerated in sensor NLRs over evolutionary time.
evidence: The abstract states this observation, which is supported by phylogenetic and sequence analysis in the results.

claim: The MADA motif has degenerated in sensor NLRs over evolutionary time.
source: NRC-dependent sensor NLRs lack MADA sequences indicating that this motif has degenerated in sensor NLRs over evolutionary time.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the abstract based on the observation that sensor NLRs lack the MADA motif.

claim: A total of 65 truncated NRC4DV::Mu-STOP variants were generated and expressed in Nicotiana benthamiana leaves.
source: We generated a total of 65 truncated NRC4DV::Mu-STOP variants and expressed these mutants in Nicotiana benthamiana leaves using agroinfiltration (Figure 1A).
evidence: The results section explicitly states the number of variants generated and tested.

claim: Only a single truncate carrying the N-terminal 29 amino acids of NRC4 triggered visible cell death in N. benthamiana leaves.
source: Remarkably, only a single truncate carrying the N-terminal 29 amino acids triggered visible cell death in N. benthamiana leaves (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The results section states this finding, which is supported by the images in Figure 1.

claim: NRC41-29-YFP triggered a visible cell death response, although the cell death intensity was weaker than that of the full-length NRC4DV-YFP.
source: NRC41-29-YFP triggered a visible cell death response, although the cell death intensity was weaker than that of the full-length NRC4DV-YFP (Figure 2B–E).
evidence: The results section describes this observation, which is supported by the images and quantification in Figure 2.

claim: The activity of the N-terminal 29 amino acids of NRC4 is independent of a full-length NRC4 protein.
source: In these plants, NRC41-29-YFP still induced cell death indicating that the activity of the N-terminal 29 amino acids of NRC4 is independent of a full-length NRC4 protein (Figure 2C–D and F–G).
evidence: The results section states this finding based on experiments in NRC4 knockout plants.

claim: YFP-mediated self-assembly is a key step in the capacity of NRC41-29-YFP to trigger hypersensitive cell death.
source: This result indicates that YFP-mediated self-assembly is a key step in the capacity of NRC41-29-YFP to trigger hypersensitive cell death.
evidence: The results section states this interpretation based on experiments with the YFPA206K mutation.

claim: The YFPA206K mutation compromised the cell death intensity of NRC41-29-YFP but not that of full-length NRC4DV.
source: The YFPA206K mutation compromised the cell death intensity of NRC41-29-YFP but not that of full-length NRC4DV (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–E).
evidence: The results section describes this observation, which is supported by the data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: A sequence database containing 988 putative CC-NLRs and CCR-NLRs was compiled from six representative plant species.
source: We first compiled a sequence database containing 988 putative CC-NLRs and CCR-NLRs (referred to from here on as CC-NLR database, Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) from six representative plant species (Arabidopsis, sugar beet, tomato, N. benthamiana, rice and barley) amended with 23 functionally characterized NLRs.
evidence: The results section describes the database compilation.

claim: The 988 proteins clustered into 59 families of at least two sequences (tribes) and 43 singletons.
source: The 988 proteins clustered into 59 families of at least two sequences (tribes) and 43 singletons (Figure 3B).
evidence: The results section states this finding from the Tribe-MCL analysis.

claim: Tribe 1 consists of 219 monocot NLRs and seven dicot NLRs.
source: The largest tribe, Tribe 1, consists of 219 monocot NLRs, including MLA10, Sr33, Sr50, the paired Pik and Pia (RGA4 and RGA5) NLRs, and seven dicot NLRs notably RPM1 (Figure 3B).
evidence: The results section describes the composition of Tribe 1.

claim: Tribe 2 consists primarily of dicot proteins (93 out of 102) but includes nine monocot NLRs.
source: Tribe 2, the second largest tribe with 102 proteins, consists primarily of dicot proteins (93 out of 102) but still includes nine monocot NLRs.
evidence: The results section describes the composition of Tribe 2.

claim: Tribe 2 grouped NRC-H proteins with well-known CC-NLRs such as ZAR1, RPP13, R2 and Rpi-vnt1.3.
source: Interestingly, Tribe 2 grouped NRC-H proteins, including NRC4, with well-known CC-NLRs, such as ZAR1, RPP13, R2 and Rpi-vnt1.3 indicating that these proteins share similarities in their CC domains (Figure 3B).
evidence: The results section states this observation from the Tribe-MCL analysis.

claim: The clustering of NLRs into N-terminal tribes does not always match the NB-ARC phylogenetic clades.
source: These analyses revealed that the clustering of NLRs into the N-terminal tribes does not always match the NB-ARC phylogenetic clades (Figure 3C).
evidence: The results section states this observation from comparing Tribe-MCL and phylogenetic analyses.

claim: There are N-terminal domain sequences that have remained conserved over evolutionary time across distantly related CC-NLRs.
source: We conclude that there are N-terminal domain sequences that have remained conserved over evolutionary time across distantly related CC-NLRs.
evidence: The results section states this conclusion based on the phylogenetic and clustering analyses.

claim: A motif conserved at the N terminus of 87 of 102 Tribe 2 proteins overlapped with the N-terminal 29 amino acids of NRC4.
source: Within Tribe 2, a motif that is conserved at the N terminus of 87 of 102 proteins overlapped with the N-terminal 29 amino acids of NRC4 we identified as sufficient to cause cell death (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The results section describes this finding from the MEME analysis.

claim: The conserved sequence pattern of the very N-terminal motif matched the ZAR1 α1 helix.
source: Remarkably, the conserved sequence pattern of this very N-terminal motif matched the ZAR1 α1 helix that undergoes a conformational switch during activation of the ZAR1 resistosome (Wang et al., 2019b) (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: The results section states this observation, which is supported by sequence alignment and structural modeling.

claim: 8 of the first 17 amino acids of ZAR1 are invariant in NRC4.
source: In fact, 8 of the first 17 amino acids of ZAR1 are invariant in NRC4, and the majority of the amino acid polymorphisms between ZAR1 and NRC4 in the α1 helix region are conservative (Figure 4A).
evidence: The results section states this observation from sequence alignment.

claim: The majority of the amino acid polymorphisms between ZAR1 and NRC4 in the α1 helix region are conservative.
source: In fact, 8 of the first 17 amino acids of ZAR1 are invariant in NRC4, and the majority of the amino acid polymorphisms between ZAR1 and NRC4 in the α1 helix region are conservative (Figure 4A).
evidence: The results section states this observation from sequence alignment.

claim: The MADA motif is mainly found in NLR proteins compared with non-NLR proteins.
source: HMMER searches revealed that the MADA motif is mainly found in NLR proteins compared with non-NLR proteins (Figure 4C).
evidence: The results section states this finding from HMMER searches of proteomes.

claim: An HMM score cut-off of 10.0 clearly distinguishes NLR proteins from others with 97.1% (34 out of 35) tomato proteins and 97.7% (42 out of 43) Arabidopsis proteins scoring over 10.0 being annotated as NLRs.
source: An HMM score cut-off of 10.0 clearly distinguishes NLR proteins from others with 97.1% (34 out of 35) tomato proteins and 97.7% (42 out of 43) Arabidopsis proteins scoring over 10.0 being annotated as NLRs (Figure 4C).
evidence: The results section provides this quantitative finding from HMMER analysis.

claim: The MADA motif is a sequence signature of a subset of NLR proteins.
source: We conclude that the MADA motif is a sequence signature of a subset of NLR proteins and that a HMMER cut-off score of 10.0 is most optimal for high confidence searches of MADA containing CC-NLR proteins (MADA-CC-NLRs).
evidence: The results section states this conclusion based on HMMER analysis.

claim: 103 hits (10.4%) were identified over the cut-off score of 10.0 when the CC-NLR database was screened using HMMER.
source: We re-screened the CC-NLR database using HMMER and identified 103 hits (10.4%) over the cut-off score of 10.0 (Figure 5A–B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The results section provides this quantitative finding from HMMER analysis.

claim: Another 129 NLRs were positive but with a score lower than 10.0, termed MADA-like CC-NLRs (MADAL-CC-NLRs).
source: We also noted that another 129 NLRs were positive but with a score lower than 10.0, and we tentatively termed these hits as MADA-like CC-NLRs (MADAL-CC-NLRs) (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The results section describes this classification based on HMMER scores.

claim: Most of the MADA hits are from dicot plant species whereas MADAL-CC-NLRs are primarily from monocots.
source: Most of the MADA hits are from dicot plant species whereas MADAL-CC-NLRs are primarily from monocots possibly reflecting a bias in our HMM profile which was built from the dicot enriched Tribe 2 (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The results section states this observation and provides a possible explanation.

claim: The majority of MADA hits (85 out of 103) were from Tribe 2.
source: Indeed, the majority of MADA hits (85 out of 103) were from Tribe 2, which includes NRC4 and ZAR1, but some MADA hits were also from other Tribes, notably the rice helper NLR Pik-2 from Tribe 1 (HMM score = 10.4) (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The results section provides this quantitative finding.

claim: The majority of the predicted MADA and MADAL motifs (199 out of 232, 85.8%) occurred at the very beginning of the NLR protein.
source: The majority of the predicted MADA and MADAL motifs (199 out of 232, 85.8%) occurred at the very beginning of the NLR protein.
evidence: The results section provides this quantitative finding about motif position.

claim: 199 out 988 (20.1%) of the CC-NLRs of six representative dicot and monocot species contain a MADA or MADAL motif at their very N-termini.
source: In summary, our bioinformatic analyses revealed that 199 out 988 (20.1%) of the CC-NLRs of six representative dicot and monocot species contain a MADA or MADAL motif at their very N-termini.
evidence: The results section provides this quantitative summary of the bioinformatic analysis.

claim: All NRC-H mapped to Tribe 2, while NRC-S clustered into eight different tribes.
source: Whereas all NRC-H mapped to Tribe 2, NRC-S clustered into eight different tribes (Figure 6A).
evidence: The results section states this observation from the Tribe-MCL analysis.

claim: The N-terminal sequences of NRC-S have diversified throughout evolutionary time.
source: This pattern indicates that unlike the NRCs, the N-terminal sequences of their NRC-S mates have diversified throughout evolutionary time.
evidence: The results section states this interpretation based on the clustering pattern.

claim: 20 out of 22 NRC-H have a predicted MADA motif at their N-termini.
source: Whereas 20 out of 22 NRC-H have a predicted MADA motif at their N-termini, none of the 117 examined NRC-S were predicted as MADA-CC-NLR in the HMMER search (Figure 6B).
evidence: The results section provides this quantitative finding.

claim: None of the 117 examined NRC-S were predicted as MADA-CC-NLR in the HMMER search.
source: Whereas 20 out of 22 NRC-H have a predicted MADA motif at their N-termini, none of the 117 examined NRC-S were predicted as MADA-CC-NLR in the HMMER search (Figure 6B).
evidence: The results section provides this quantitative finding.

claim: 65 of 117 NRC-S have N-terminal extensions of ~600 amino acids prior to their predicted CC domains.
source: In fact, 65 of 117 NRC-S, including the well know disease resistance proteins R1, Prf, Sw5b, Hero, Rpi-blb2 and Mi-1.2, have N-terminal extensions of ~600 amino acids, or more in the case of Prf, prior to their predicted CC domains (Figure 6B).
evidence: The results section provides this quantitative finding about NRC-S domain architecture.

claim: The CC domains of NRCs and their NRC-S mates have experienced distinct evolutionary trajectories.
source: These findings indicate the CC domains of NRCs and their NRC-S mates have experienced distinct evolutionary trajectories even though these NLR proteins share a common evolutionary origin.
evidence: The results section states this interpretation based on the phylogenetic and sequence analyses.

claim: The L9A/V10A/L14A mutation significantly reduced, but did not abolish, NRC4DV cell death inducing activity.
source: We introduced a triple alanine substitution similar to the mutant of Wang et al. (2019b) into the autoactive NRC4DV and found that this L9A/V10A/L14A mutation significantly reduced, but did not abolish, NRC4DV cell death inducing activity (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: The results section describes this observation from mutagenesis experiments.

claim: The L9E/V10E/L14E mutation resulted in a more severe disruption of the cell death activity of NRC4DV compared to the triple alanine mutant.
source: Therefore, we substituted L9, V10 and L14 with glutamic acid, and observed that the L9E/V10E/L14E mutation resulted in a more severe disruption of the cell death activity of NRC4DV compared to the triple alanine mutant (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: The results section describes this observation from mutagenesis experiments.

claim: Both of the NRC4DV triple alanine and glutamic acid mutant proteins accumulated to similar levels as NRC4DV when expressed in N. benthamiana leaves.
source: Both of the NRC4DV triple alanine and glutamic acid mutant proteins accumulated to similar levels as NRC4DV when expressed in N. benthamiana leaves indicating that the observed loss-of-function phenotypes were not due to protein destabilization (Figure 7D).
evidence: The results section states this observation from immunoblot analysis.

claim: The triple alanine mutation abolished the cell death triggered by both NRC41-29-YFP and ZAR11-144-YFP.
source: The triple alanine mutation abolished the cell death triggered by both NRC41-29-YFP and ZAR11-144-YFP, supporting the view that MADA motifs are essential for the capacity of the N-termini of NRC4 and ZAR1 to cause cell death (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: The results section describes this observation from mutagenesis experiments.

claim: None of the tested single alanine-substituted mutants affected the cell death response of NRC4DV.
source: None of the tested single alanine-substituted mutants affected the cell death response of NRC4DV (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The results section states this observation from mutagenesis experiments.

claim: Single glutamic acid mutations L9E, L13E and L17E essentially abolished the cell death activity of NRC4DV without affecting the stability of the mutant proteins.
source: In contrast, single glutamic acid mutations L9E, L13E and L17E essentially abolished the cell death activity of NRC4DV without affecting the stability of the mutant proteins (Figure 8).
evidence: The results section describes this observation from mutagenesis experiments.

claim: The L9, L13, and L17 residues in the MADA motif are critical for cell death induction by NRC4.
source: Therefore, we determined that the L9, L13, and L17 residues in the MADA motif are critical for cell death induction by NRC4.
evidence: The results section states this conclusion based on mutagenesis experiments.

claim: L9, L13 and L17 mapped to the outer surface of the funnel-shaped structure formed by the α1 helices in a homology model of the CC domain of NRC4.
source: All three residues mapped to the outer surface of the funnel-shaped structure formed by the α1 helices similar to the previously identified residues in positions 9, 10 and 14.
evidence: The results section describes this observation from structural modeling.

claim: The outer surface of the funnel-shaped structure formed by N-terminal helices is critical for the function of both ZAR1 and NRC4.
source: These results suggest that the outer surface of the funnel-shaped structure formed by N-terminal helices is critical not only for the function of ZAR1 but also for the activity of another MADA-CC-NLR.
evidence: The results section states this interpretation based on mutagenesis and structural modeling.

claim: NRC41-29-YFP produced fluorescence signal in punctate structures throughout the cell in addition to relatively weak nucleocytoplasmic signal.
source: Interestingly, unlike free YFP which typically shows nucleocytoplasmic distribution, NRC41-29-YFP produced fluorescence signal in punctate structures throughout the cell in addition to relatively weak nucleocytoplasmic signal (Figure 9A).
evidence: The results section describes this observation from microscopy experiments.

claim: Some of the NRC41-29-YFP puncta associated with the plasma membrane.
source: Although the NRC41-29-YFP puncta did not completely overlap with RFP-Rem1.3 signal, we noticed some of the NRC41-29-YFP puncta associated with the plasma membrane (Figure 9A–B).
evidence: The results section describes this observation from microscopy experiments.

claim: NRC41-29-YFPA206K rarely formed puncta.
source: In contrast to NRC41-29-YFP, NRC41-29-YFPA206K rarely formed puncta (Figure 9A,C), suggesting that YFP self-assembly is required for NRC41-29-YFP puncta formation.
evidence: The results section describes this observation from microscopy experiments.

claim: YFP self-assembly is required for NRC41-29-YFP puncta formation.
source: In contrast to NRC41-29-YFP, NRC41-29-YFPA206K rarely formed puncta (Figure 9A,C), suggesting that YFP self-assembly is required for NRC41-29-YFP puncta formation.
evidence: The results section states this interpretation based on the YFPA206K mutation experiment.

claim: Introducing the L9E in NRC41-29-YFP greatly reduced puncta formation.
source: Furthermore, introducing the L9E in NRC41-29-YFP greatly reduced puncta formation (Figure 9A,C).
evidence: The results section describes this observation from microscopy experiments.

claim: Both an intact MADA motif and YFP oligomerization are required for the capacity of NRC41-29-YFP to form puncta as well as cause cell death in N. benthamiana leaves.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that both an intact MADA motif and YFP oligomerization are required for the capacity of NRC41-29-YFP to form puncta as well as cause cell death in N. benthamiana leaves.
evidence: The results section states this conclusion based on the microscopy and cell death experiments.

claim: The ZAR11-17-NRC4 chimeric protein can trigger cell death in N. benthamiana leaves.
source: The resulting ZAR11-17-NRC4 chimeric protein can still trigger cell death in N. benthamiana leaves indicating that the MADA/α1 helix sequence is functionally equivalent between these two NLR proteins (Figure 10C, Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The results section describes this observation from chimera experiments.

claim: The MADA/α1 helix sequence is functionally equivalent between NRC4 and ZAR1.
source: The resulting ZAR11-17-NRC4 chimeric protein can still trigger cell death in N. benthamiana leaves indicating that the MADA/α1 helix sequence is functionally equivalent between these two NLR proteins (Figure 10C, Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The results section states this interpretation based on the chimera experiments.

claim: All of the assayed chimeric NRC4DV proteins with MADA sequences from NRC2, RPP8, RPP13, Pik-2, and Os03g30910.1 retained the capacity to trigger cell death in N. benthamiana leaves.
source: All of the assayed chimeric NRC4DV proteins retained the capacity to trigger cell death in N. benthamiana leaves (Figure 10C, Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The results section describes this observation from chimera experiments.

claim: NRC4DV chimeras with MADAL sequences from Arabidopsis RPM1 and barley MLA10 retained the capacity to trigger cell death.
source: Both NRC4DV chimeras retained the capacity to trigger cell death indicating that these MADAL sequences are functionally analogous to the NRC4 N-terminus (Figure 10C, Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The results section describes this observation from chimera experiments.

claim: The MADAL sequences from RPM1 and MLA10 are functionally analogous to the NRC4 N-terminus.
source: Both NRC4DV chimeras retained the capacity to trigger cell death indicating that these MADAL sequences are functionally analogous to the NRC4 N-terminus (Figure 10C, Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The results section states this interpretation based on the chimera experiments.

claim: The MADA motif is functionally conserved even between distantly related NLRs from dicots and monocots.
source: These results indicate that the MADA motif is functionally conserved even between distantly related NLRs from dicots and monocots.
evidence: The results section states this conclusion based on the chimera experiments.

claim: The N-termini of Bs2 and LOV1 did not complement the cell death activity when swapped into NRC4DV.
source: Interestingly, whereas the N-termini of Bs2 and LOV1 did not complement the cell death activity when swapped into NRC4DV, Rx1-17 could confer cell death activity when swapped into NRC4DV (Figure 10C, Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The results section describes this observation from chimera experiments.

claim: Rx1-17 could confer cell death activity when swapped into NRC4DV.
source: Interestingly, whereas the N-termini of Bs2 and LOV1 did not complement the cell death activity when swapped into NRC4DV, Rx1-17 could confer cell death activity when swapped into NRC4DV (Figure 10C, Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The results section describes this observation from chimera experiments.

claim: At least one of the N-terminal sequences that are not predicted as having the MADA motif may still functionally complement the N-terminus of NRC4.
source: This exception indicates that at least one of the N-terminal sequences that are not predicted as having the MADA motif may still functionally complement the N-terminus of NRC4.
evidence: The results section states this interpretation based on the Rx chimera result.

claim: The NRC4 L9A/V10A/L14A and L9E mutants failed to rescue the resistance to P. infestans in the N. benthamiana nrc4a/b_9.1.3 mutant.
source: Unlike wild-type NRC4, the NRC4 L9A/V10A/L14A and L9E mutants failed to rescue the resistance to P. infestans in the N. benthamiana nrc4a/b_9.1.3 mutant, indicating that MADA motif mutations not only impair HR cell death as shown above but also affect disease resistance against an oomycete pathogen (Figure 11B).
evidence: The results section describes this observation from pathogen infection assays.

claim: MADA motif mutations not only impair HR cell death but also affect disease resistance against an oomycete pathogen.
source: Unlike wild-type NRC4, the NRC4 L9A/V10A/L14A and L9E mutants failed to rescue the resistance to P. infestans in the N. benthamiana nrc4a/b_9.1.3 mutant, indicating that MADA motif mutations not only impair HR cell death as shown above but also affect disease resistance against an oomycete pathogen (Figure 11B).
evidence: The results section states this interpretation based on the pathogen infection assays.

claim: ZAR11-17-NRC4 complemented the nrc4a/b_9.1.3 N. benthamiana mutant to a similar degree as wild-type NRC4.
source: We conducted similar complementation assays with the ZAR11-17-NRC4 chimera in which the first 17 amino acids of NRC4 were swapped with the equivalent region of ZAR1, and found that ZAR11-17-NRC4 complemented the nrc4a/b_9.1.3 N. benthamiana mutant to a similar degree as wild-type NRC4 (Figure 11B).
evidence: The results section describes this observation from pathogen infection assays.

claim: The chimeric ZAR11-17-NRC4 is able to trigger HR cell death and retains its capacity to function with its NRC-S mate Rpi-blb2 and confer resistance to P. infestans.
source: These experiments further confirm that the α1 helix/MADA motif of Arabidopsis ZAR1 is functionally equivalent to the N-terminus of NRC4, and that the chimeric ZAR11-17-NRC4 is not only able to trigger HR cell death but also retains its capacity to function with its NRC-S mate Rpi-blb2 and confer resistance to P. infestans.
evidence: The results section states this conclusion based on the pathogen infection assays.

claim: The ZAR1 'death switch' mechanism may apply to NRCs and other MADA-CC-NLRs from dicot and monocot plant species.
source: Our finding that the ZAR1 α1 helix/MADA motif can functionally replace its matching region in NRC4 indicates that the ZAR1 'death switch' mechanism may apply to NRCs and other MADA-CC-NLRs from dicot and monocot plant species.
evidence: The discussion section states this interpretation based on the functional complementation experiments.

claim: MADA-type sequences have emerged early in the evolution of CC-NLRs and have remained conserved from singletons to helpers in NLR pair and network throughout evolution.
source: In this model, we propose that MADA-type sequences have emerged early in the evolution of CC-NLRs and have remained conserved from singletons to helpers in NLR pair and network throughout evolution.
evidence: The discussion section proposes this evolutionary model based on the phylogenetic and functional data.

claim: MADA sequences appear to have degenerated over time in sensor CC-NLRs as these proteins specialized in pathogen detection and lost the capacity to execute the immune response without their helper mates.
source: In sharp contrast, MADA sequences appear to have degenerated over time in sensor CC-NLRs as these proteins specialized in pathogen detection and lost the capacity to execute the immune response without their helper mates.
evidence: The discussion section proposes this evolutionary model based on the observation that sensor NLRs lack MADA motifs.

claim: NRC-H are more highly conserved than their NRC-S partners within the Solanaceae.
source: Consistent with this view, NRC-H are known to be more highly conserved than their NRC-S partners within the Solanaceae (Wu et al., 2017; Stam et al., 2019).
evidence: The discussion section cites previous studies to support the evolutionary model.

claim: The N-terminal domains of Prf and Sw5b function as baits that sense pathogen effectors.
source: In fact, the N-terminal domains of Prf and Sw5b function as baits that sense pathogen effectors, suggesting functional analogy to integrated effector detection motifs found in some NLRs, and are not known to be involved in executing the immune response (Saur et al., 2015; Li et al., 2019a).
evidence: The discussion section cites previous studies about the function of N-terminal domains in sensor NLRs.

claim: The CC domains of sensor NLRs have extensively diversified over evolutionary time and are losing the capacity to function as HR cell death executors.
source: Here, we hypothesize that the CC domains of these and other sensor NLRs have extensively diversified over evolutionary time and are losing the capacity to function as HR cell death executors.
evidence: The discussion section proposes this hypothesis based on the evolutionary model.

claim: The NB domain of Rx was reported to be capable of triggering cell death.
source: Nonetheless, previously the NB domain of Rx was reported to be capable of triggering cell death (Rairdan et al., 2008), suggesting that the CC domain of Rx is dispensable for activation of HR.
evidence: The discussion section cites a previous study about Rx function.

claim: The CC domain of Rx is dispensable for activation of HR.
source: Nonetheless, previously the NB domain of Rx was reported to be capable of triggering cell death (Rairdan et al., 2008), suggesting that the CC domain of Rx is dispensable for activation of HR.
evidence: The discussion section states this interpretation based on a previous study.

claim: The N-termini of some NRC-S may not have fully degenerated into non-functional sequences and may have residual ability to functionally complement MADA.
source: Therefore, in our 'use-it-or-lose-it' model, the N-termini of some NRC-S may not have fully degenerated into non-functional sequences and may have residual ability to functionally complement MADA.
evidence: The discussion section proposes this interpretation to explain the Rx chimera result.

claim: Only Pik-2 was detected to carry an N-terminal MADA motif among the Pik-1 and Pik-2 pair.
source: In our computational analyses only Pik-2 was detected to carry an N-terminal MADA motif (Figure 5, HMM score = 10.4) even though the CC domains of both proteins grouped into Tribe 1 (Figure 3).
evidence: The discussion section states this observation from the computational analysis.

claim: The Pik-2 MADA motif could substitute for the N-terminus of NRC4 in cell death assays despite having six additional amino-acids at its N-terminus.
source: The Pik-2 MADA motif could substitute for the N-terminus of NRC4 in our cell death assays despite having six additional amino-acids at its N-terminus (Figure 10).
evidence: The discussion section states this observation from the chimera experiments.

claim: The helper NLR Pik-2 may execute HR cell death via its N-terminal MADA motif whereas its paired sensor NLR Pik-1 does not have the capacity to carry this activity on its own.
source: These results are consistent with our Figure 11 model and imply that the helper NLR Pik-2 may execute HR cell death via its N-terminal MADA motif whereas its paired sensor NLR Pik-1 does not have the capacity to carry this activity on its own.
evidence: The discussion section states this interpretation based on the Pik-1/Pik-2 analysis.

claim: Four of the five RPP8 paralogs in the Arabidopsis ecotype Col-0 were deemed to have a MADA motif based on HMMER searches.
source: Four of the five RPP8 paralogs in the Arabidopsis ecotype Col-0 were deemed to have a MADA motif based on our HMMER searches, whereas a fifth paralog LOV1 (AT1G10920) was negative and did not complement NRC4 autoactivity in the MADA motif swap experiments (Figure 10, Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The discussion section states this observation from the computational and experimental analyses.

claim: LOV1 confers sensitivity to the victorin effector produced by the necrotrophic fungus Cochliobolus victoriae by binding the defense-associated thioredoxin TRX-h5 when it is complexed with victorin.
source: LOV1 confers sensitivity to the victorin effector produced by the necrotrophic fungus Cochliobolus victoriae by binding the defense-associated thioredoxin TRX-h5 when it is complexed with victorin (Lorang et al., 2012).
evidence: The discussion section cites a previous study about LOV1 function.

claim: LOV1 binds TRX-h5 via its CC domain.
source: Interestingly, LOV1 binds TRX-h5 via its CC domain indicating that this region has evolved a pathogen sensor activity in this NLR protein (Lorang et al., 2012).
evidence: The discussion section cites a previous study about LOV1 function.

claim: The CC domain of LOV1 has evolved a pathogen sensor activity.
source: Interestingly, LOV1 binds TRX-h5 via its CC domain indicating that this region has evolved a pathogen sensor activity in this NLR protein (Lorang et al., 2012).
evidence: The discussion section states this interpretation based on a previous study.

claim: In activated ZAR1 resistosome, a funnel-shaped structure formed by five α1 helices is thought to directly execute hypersensitive cell death by forming a toxin-like pore in the plasma membrane.
source: In activated ZAR1 resistosome, a funnel-shaped structure formed by five α1 helices is thought to directly execute hypersensitive cell death by forming a toxin-like pore in the plasma membrane (Wang et al., 2019b).
evidence: The discussion section cites the ZAR1 model from a previous study.

claim: Structure informed mutagenesis of ZAR1 revealed that F9, L10 and L14 on the outer surface of the funnel-shaped structure are required for immunity.
source: Structure informed mutagenesis of ZAR1 revealed that F9, L10 and L14 on the outer surface of the funnel-shaped structure are required for immunity (Wang et al., 2019b).
evidence: The discussion section cites findings from a previous study on ZAR1.

claim: The ZAR1 double mutant E11A/E18A is impaired in cell death and disease resistance activities.
source: As discussed by Wang et al. (2019b), the interior space of the funnel structure is also important because the ZAR1 double mutant E11A/E18A is impaired in cell death and disease resistance activities.
evidence: The discussion section cites findings from a previous study on ZAR1.

claim: A subset of CC-NLRs of the RPW8/HR family have a distinct type of coiled-coil domain known as CCR.
source: A subset of CC-NLRs of the RPW8/HR family of atypical resistance proteins have a distinct type of coiled-coil domain known as CCR (Barragan et al., 2019; Li et al., 2019b).
evidence: The discussion section cites previous studies about CCR-NLRs.

claim: No MADA type sequences were detected in CCR-NLR proteins.
source: We failed to detect any MADA type sequences in these CCR-NLR proteins.
evidence: The discussion section states this observation from the computational analysis.

claim: The CCR domain has similarity to mixed lineage kinase domain-like (MLKL) proteins and fungal HeLo/HELL domains, which form multi-helix bundles and act as membrane pore forming toxins.
source: Indeed, the CCR domain has similarity to mixed lineage kinase domain-like (MLKL) proteins and fungal HeLo/HELL domains, which form multi-helix bundles and act as membrane pore forming toxins (Barragan et al., 2019; Li et al., 2019a; Mahdi et al., 2019).
evidence: The discussion section cites previous studies about CCR domain structure and function.

claim: Arabidopsis HR4 interacts in an allele-specific manner with the genetically unlinked CC-NLR RPP7b to trigger autoimmunity in the absence of pathogens.
source: Interestingly, Arabidopsis HR4, a CCR containing protein, interacts in an allele-specific manner with the genetically unlinked CC-NLR RPP7b to trigger autoimmunity in the absence of pathogens (Barragan et al., 2019).
evidence: The discussion section cites a previous study about HR4 and RPP7b interaction.

claim: RPP7b forms higher-order complexes of six to seven subunits only when activated by the matching autoimmune HR4Fei-0 protein.
source: Recently, Li et al. (2019b) showed that RPP7b forms higher-order complexes of six to seven subunits only when activated by the matching autoimmune HR4Fei-0 protein in a biochemical process reminiscent of activated ZAR1 resistosome (Li et al., 2019a).
evidence: The discussion section cites a previous study about RPP7b complex formation.

claim: RPP7b and its four Arabidopsis paralogs were all classed as carrying the MADA motif in HMMER searches.
source: In our HMMER searches, RPP7b and its four Arabidopsis paralogs were all classed as carrying the MADA motif.
evidence: The discussion section states this observation from the computational analysis.

claim: Findings by Li et al. (2019b) directly link a MADA-CC-NLR to the formation of resistosome type structures.
source: Thus, findings by Li et al. (2019b) directly link a MADA-CC-NLR to the formation of resistosome type structures consistent with our view that the ZAR1 model widely applies to other NLRs with the MADA α1 helix.
evidence: The discussion section states this interpretation connecting previous findings to the current study.

claim: The discovery of the MADA motif as a signature of NLR singletons and helpers enables the development of computational pipelines for predicting NLR networks from naïve plant genomes.
source: It has not escaped our attention that the discovery of the MADA motif as a signature of NLR singletons and helpers—but missing in sensor NLRs—enables the development of computational pipelines for predicting NLR networks from naïve plant genomes.
evidence: The discussion section proposes this application of the MADA motif discovery.

claim: Dissecting the NLR network architecture of plant species has direct implications for breeding disease resistance into crop plants and reducing the autoimmune load of NLRs.
source: Dissecting the NLR network architecture of plant species is not only useful for basic mechanistic studies but has also direct implications for breeding disease resistance into crop plants and reducing the autoimmune load of NLRs (Chae et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2018; Adachi et al., 2019a).
evidence: The discussion section states this application and cites previous studies.

claim: NRC4 is a helper NLR that functions with multiple sensor NLRs within a Solanaceae receptor network.
source: We applied this method to NRC4—a helper NLR that functions with multiple sensor NLRs within a Solanaceae receptor network.
evidence: The abstract describes the role of NRC4 based on previous knowledge.

claim: Plant NLRs are intracellular immune receptors that detect host-translocated pathogen virulence proteins known as effectors.
source: Plants have evolved intracellular immune receptors to detect host-translocated pathogen virulence proteins, known as effectors (Dodds and Rathjen, 2010; Jones et al., 2016; Kourelis and van der Hoorn, 2018).
evidence: The introduction cites previous studies about plant NLR function.

claim: NLR-triggered immunity includes the hypersensitive response (HR), a type of programmed cell death associated with disease resistance.
source: NLR-triggered immunity (also known as effector-triggered immunity) includes the hypersensitive response (HR), a type of programmed cell death associated with disease resistance.
evidence: The introduction describes NLR-triggered immunity based on established knowledge.

claim: Plants express very large and diverse repertoires of NLRs, with anywhere from about 50 to 1000 genes encoded per genome.
source: In contrast to other taxa, plants express very large and diverse repertoires of NLRs, with anywhere from about 50 to 1000 genes encoded per genome (Shao et al., 2016; Steuernagel et al., 2018).
evidence: The introduction cites previous studies about NLR repertoire sizes.

claim: Plant NLRs form receptor networks with varying degrees of complexity.
source: An emerging paradigm is that plant NLRs form receptor networks with varying degrees of complexity (Wu et al., 2018).
evidence: The introduction cites a previous study about NLR networks.

claim: Plant NLRs have probably evolved from multifunctional singleton receptors to functionally specialized interconnected receptor pairs and networks.
source: NLRs have probably evolved from multifunctional singleton receptors—which combine pathogen detection (sensor activity) and immune signalling (helper or executor activity) into a single protein—to functionally specialized interconnected receptor pairs and networks (Adachi et al., 2019a).
evidence: The introduction cites a previous study proposing this evolutionary model.

claim: Most plant NLRs have characteristic N-terminal domains that define three subgroups: coiled-coil (CC), CCR or RPW8-like (RPW8) and toll and interleukin-1 receptor (TIR).
source: In addition to the NB and LRR domains, most plant NLRs have characteristic N-terminal domains that define three subgroups: coiled-coil (CC), CCR or RPW8-like (RPW8) and toll and interleukin-1 receptor (TIR) (Shao et al., 2016).
evidence: The introduction cites a previous study about NLR classification.

claim: In metazoans, NLRs confer immunity to diverse pathogens through a wheel-like oligomerization process resulting in multiprotein platforms that recruit downstream elements, such as caspases.
source: In metazoans, NLRs confer immunity to diverse pathogens through a wheel-like oligomerization process resulting in multiprotein platforms that recruit downstream elements, such as caspases (Qi et al., 2010; Zhou et al., 2015; Hu et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2015; Tenthorey et al., 2017).
evidence: The introduction cites previous studies about metazoan NLR function.

claim: Wang et al. (2019a) and Wang et al. (2019b) reconstituted the inactive and active complexes of the Arabidopsis CC-NLR ZAR1 with its partner receptor-like cytoplasmic kinases (RLCKs).
source: They reconstituted the inactive and active complexes of the Arabidopsis CC-NLR ZAR1 (HOPZ-ACTIVATED RESISTANCE1) with its partner receptor-like cytoplasmic kinases (RLCKs) (Wang et al., 2019a; Wang et al., 2019b).
evidence: The introduction cites previous studies about ZAR1 structure.

claim: Activated ZAR1 forms a resistosome—a wheel-like pentamer that undergoes a conformational switch to expose a funnel-shaped structure formed by the N-terminal α helices (α1) of the CC domains.
source: Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures revealed that activated ZAR1 forms a resistosome—a wheel-like pentamer that undergoes a conformational switch to expose a funnel-shaped structure formed by the N-terminal α helices (α1) of the CC domains (Wang et al., 2019a; Wang et al., 2019b).
evidence: The introduction cites previous studies about ZAR1 resistosome structure.

claim: The exposed α1 helices of the ZAR1 resistosome mediate cell death by translocating into the plasma membrane and perturbing membrane integrity similar to pore-forming toxins.
source: They propose an engaging model in which the exposed α1 helices of the ZAR1 resistosome mediate cell death by translocating into the plasma membrane and perturbing membrane integrity similar to pore-forming toxins (Wang et al., 2019b).
evidence: The introduction cites the model proposed by Wang et al. (2019b).

claim: Paired and networked NLRs consist of sensor NLRs that detect pathogen effectors and helper NLRs that translate this effector recognition into HR cell death and immunity.
source: Paired and networked NLRs consist of sensor NLRs that detect pathogen effectors and helper NLRs that translate this effector recognition into HR cell death and immunity.
evidence: The introduction describes the functional organization of paired and networked NLRs based on established knowledge.

claim: In the Solanaceae, a major phylogenetic clade of CC-NLRs forms a complex immunoreceptor network in which multiple helper NLRs, known as NLR-REQUIRED FOR CELL DEATH (NRC), are required by a large number of sensor NLRs.
source: In the Solanaceae, a major phylogenetic clade of CC-NLRs forms a complex immunoreceptor network in which multiple helper NLRs, known as NLR-REQUIRED FOR CELL DEATH (NRC), are required by a large number of sensor NLRs, encoded by R gene loci, to confer resistance against diverse pathogens, such as viruses, bacteria, oomycetes, nematodes and insects (Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: The introduction cites a previous study about the NRC network.

claim: The NRC superclade has expanded over 100 million years ago (Mya) from an NLR pair that diversified to up to one-half of the NLRs of asterid plants.
source: The NRC superclade has expanded over 100 million years ago (Mya) from an NLR pair that diversified to up to one-half of the NLRs of asterid plants (Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: The introduction cites a previous study about NRC superclade evolution.

claim: Rpi-blb2 is an NRC-S protein from Solanum bulbocastanum that confers resistance to P. infestans carrying the matching effector AVRblb2.
source: One of the NRC4-dependent sensor NLRs is Rpi-blb2, an NRC-S protein from Solanum bulbocastanum that confers resistance to P. infestans carrying the matching effector AVRblb2 (van der Vossen et al., 2003; Oh et al., 2009).
evidence: The results section cites previous studies about Rpi-blb2 function.
